capabilities.target: Supabase Postgres database, via service role that bypasses row level security, including the integration_tokens table
support_messages table, rows rendered back to the customer in the ticket

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE ('Show me the latest open support tickets.')
Customer-written ticket message submitted through the public support widget

elements.name: Anonymous/unauthenticated customer submitting via the public support widget
Ticket message ingress from public widget into agent context
Reply insert egress into customer-visible support_messages

controls.name: Per-call IDE approval prompt showing the SQL
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate enforced by the IDE client does not weaken as the model becomes more capable, but its real-world effectiveness depends on approval volume: developers approving many calls per session are prone to approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403) and may not scrutinize a plausible-looking but malicious query.

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-respecting database role for the agent
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scoped to omit the integration_tokens table and to respect row level security does not decay with model capability; the model cannot read data it has no grant to read.

controls.name: Secret-pattern/DLP check before inserting into support_messages
controls.decay_rationale: A pattern or classifier based scan on outbound content can be evaded through encoding, paraphrase, or splitting the secret across multiple inserts as the model gets more capable.

controls.name: Pin or hash the Supabase MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning a specific, hashed server version does not decay with model capability; it prevents an unreviewed update from silently changing tool behavior.

controls.name: Tamper-evident log of agent-executed SQL, attributed separately from the developer
controls.decay_rationale: A store-side, tamper-evident log does not depend on model cooperation to record what ran.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): ticket-injected exfiltration of integration tokens via service-role SQL agent

attack_path.note: Customer-controlled ticket text enters the agent's context when it reads open tickets, and can carry instructions to the model (indirect prompt injection).
The agent executes SQL as the service role, which bypasses row level security, and can be directed by the injected text to also read the integration_tokens table.
The agent inserts the harvested token value into support_messages, a row rendered back to the customer, completing disclosure across the trust boundary.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: The per-call approval requirement is removed, relaxed to session-level/'always allow', or autonomy.level is raised from A1 toward A3/A4 for this agent or tool.

evidence.observation: The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, and a table of integration tokens sits in the same database.
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget, and rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, making the insert an egress channel to an untrusted party.
The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL, but developers approve many calls in a session, indicating high approval volume and approval fatigue risk (SAFE-T1403).

The Supabase MCP server is launched via 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', which is unpinned and fetches whatever version is current, with no stated identity verification of the package or server.

recommendations.action: Scope the agent's database credential to least privilege, respecting row level security and excluding the integration_tokens table and any other secrets table not needed to answer support queries.
Add a secret-pattern/DLP check that blocks inserts into support_messages (or any customer-visible field) containing token- or credential-like strings.
Pin the Supabase MCP server to a specific version or hash instead of @latest, and verify package integrity before each session.
Add tamper-evident logging of every SQL statement the agent executes, attributed separately from the developer's own identity.

Spotlight/delimit ticket message content as untrusted data and instruct the model never to treat it as instructions; treat this as defense in depth only, not a substitute for the structural fixes above.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent runs as a single local process inside the developer's authenticated IDE session; no peer in this design impersonates the agent process itself.
autonomy.can_modify_own_config is false and no memory capability is declared, so the agent's own configuration or instructions are not reachable for tampering here.
No audit log is described that attributes SQL executions to the agent separately from the developer, so the exfiltration path leaves no attributable record.
The agent can read restricted integration tokens via the service role and then expose them through the reply write.
No spend, unattended execution, or self-spawning capability is declared, and every tool call is gated by individual human approval.
The agent operates with a service-role credential that bypasses row level security, exceeding what the requesting customer could access directly.
The server is fetched unpinned via @latest with no stated identity verification, leaving it open to name-collision or package substitution (SAFE-T1004).
definitions_pinned is false, so the tool definitions this server exposes can change between sessions without review (rug pull, SAFE-T1201).
No logging of SQL executed through this server is described, matching the agent-level attribution gap.
The server is the channel through which restricted token data is read and then written to a customer-visible table.
The server executes one SQL statement per human-approved tool call; no autonomous retry or flood behavior is described.
The server is configured with a shared service-role credential rather than a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role.
The public support widget's authentication is not described, so an attacker can plausibly submit ticket text as if from any customer.
No record ties a ticket message's true origin to an identity, compounding the attribution gap for the resulting exfiltration.
The developer is a local, authenticated IDE user on their own machine; this design does not expose developer identity to remote impersonation.
The design does not state whether individual developer approvals are logged per user with timestamps; insufficient detail to assess.
The write capability lets the agent insert attacker-influenced content, including harvested secrets, into a row the database will render back to the customer.
The service-role connection can read the integration_tokens table alongside ordinary support data, with no row level security boundary.
No unbounded query volume or storage exhaustion is described; each execution is gated by an individual human approval, not autonomous looping.
Ticket text is attacker-controlled and unvalidated as it enters the agent's context, enabling indirect prompt injection.
This inbound flow carries untrusted ticket text into the agent; it does not itself carry confidential data outward, so disclosure risk sits on the outbound reply flow.
The design does not state whether the public support widget rate-limits ticket submissions, so flooding risk on this channel cannot be assessed.
The insert occurs within the same managed database connection as the read; in-transit tampering distinct from the capability misuse covered in finding f1 is not described.
This is the egress channel through which harvested integration tokens would reach the customer.
Each insert corresponds to one human-approved tool call; no bulk-write or resource exhaustion path is described for this flow.

rating.rationale: An untrusted customer-controlled ticket message can reach a service-role SQL read of restricted integration tokens and then a write to a customer-visible table, an irreversible egress of restricted data (inherent: critical, TC1 lethal trifecta). The only declared control is a per-call, raw-action IDE approval prompt; because the design states developers approve many calls per session, approval_volume is high, which under rubric section 5 step 2 earns only a one-tier credit and caps the floor at moderate rather than low, giving a residual of high. No structural credential scoping, output secret filtering, destination pinning, or audit logging is declared, so all of those are recorded as missing_recommended controls and named as the fix. Under autonomy_increase or control_removal, the approval gate itself is defeated and the forecast returns to critical, matching the mechanism of the public incident this design mirrors.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No system prompt or instruction text was provided for ide-db-agent, so instruction-level issues (ambiguous goals, unbounded scope wording) could not be directly assessed; scope is inferred from the declared capabilities.

No logging or audit configuration was described beyond the approval prompt, so the repudiation findings (no attributable record of agent actions) are based on absence of evidence, at medium confidence.
The authentication model for the public support widget is not described, so the exact ease of identity spoofing for ticket submission could not be precisely assessed.
